title: Mohnish Pabrai's Interview with Knowledge Inside podcast on August 19, 2026 - Episode 1

reader_summary.headline: Mohnish Pabrai shares investing wisdom on spending, finding cheap great companies, and avoiding crowds.
reader_summary.overview: Mohnish Pabrai advises beginners to start with index funds or Berkshire Hathaway before learning to pick individual stocks. He explains how to find overlooked businesses, like memory chip makers during an AI boom, and why holding great companies long-term is key. Pabrai also warns against using borrowed money and following the crowd.

key_points.text: Spend less than you earn first, then invest the extra money in an index fund or Berkshire Hathaway.
key_points.evidence_quote: So before we change how to invest, we should change how to spend. And the very simple change on how to spend is spend less than you earn.

key_points.text: Memory chip makers act like pickax sellers in an AI gold rush, locking in future sales with contracts.
key_points.evidence_quote: So, in effect, Levi's got its start because of the gold drives, because all the gold miners, they bought bought the jeans. And today, when we have the AI boom, the pickax makers are the memory guys.

key_points.text: Look for great companies that are cheap and overlooked, rather than famous ones that everyone already owns.
key_points.evidence_quote: So what we are looking for is a business that is great, but being overlooked. So we want to find greatness before it's universally recognized as great.

key_points.text: You should only sell a company if you are certain its decline is permanent, not just a temporary problem.
key_points.evidence_quote: Don't do anything. Don't do anything until there is clear evidence that the decline is permanent, not temporary. You have no doubt that the decline is permanent.

key_points.text: Retail investors can beat big funds by using their personal knowledge of taste and intangible brand value.
key_points.evidence_quote: In fact, we can be better than the institutional investors. Yeah. Because you have direct knowledge, you may understand things better because, you know, a lot of things better. Because, you know, a lot of things like they are based on taste or some perfume or something, you know what I'm saying.

reader_summary.why_it_matters: Understanding a company's unique strengths helps you hold it for decades without needing to do much work or worry about short-term price changes.
